evidence.quote: In 1945 it was acquired by Rayonier for their lumber operation near Forks. It was retired near the north end of Forks in Tillicum Park in 1959.

evidence.claim: a former logging railway follows the lake’s north side.

evidence.quote: The Spruce Railroad Trail follows the grade of what was once the tracks of a logging railroad along the shores of the lake. By following this trail on the north side of the lake one can find the entrance to an old railroad tunnel that is now part of the Spruce Railroad Trail

evidence.claim: The lake fills a valley carved by glaciers during the last Ice Age.
evidence.quote: The lake was formed when glaciers carved deep valleys during the last Ice Age.

evidence.claim: Low nitrogen levels limit algae growth, helping give the water its clarity and blue color.
evidence.quote: Lake Crescent is known for brilliant blue waters and exceptional clarity caused by low levels of nitrogen in the water that inhibit the growth of algae.

evidence.quote: The lake was included in the Olympic Forest Reserve in 1897, designated as a recreation area in 1921, and finally included in Olympic National Park in 1938.

flags: Tourism describes a 350-mile Olympia-to-Long Beach itinerary; the highway cache covers 366 miles from the Columbia bridge to Tumwater. The story follows the supplied bridge-to-Olympia corridor and does not assign the tourism mileage or drive-time estimate to that scope.
State scenic-byway status is supported by the highway cache and tourism pages; catalog National Forest Scenic Byway status is not explicitly confirmed.
Lake Crescent’s Klallam origin account is present only in a secondary source, with no community source cached; omitted. Geology and railroad history retained instead.
Lake Crescent depth figures and landslide chronologies differ within its cache; exact depths, dates and lake-separation claims omitted. Geology has no primary scientific source cached.
Current Forks text softened 6,000 to about 6,000 without a source hedge. Visitor totals are omitted for focus; the cache supports 6,000 plainly and nearly 73,000 by 2010.

Scenic Washington’s page contains potentially stale visitor-facility information, including Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center; those access claims are not reused. No current facility access is inferred from designation.
Ruby Beach remains below 90 words because the dedicated cache is brief; no beach activity or present access details were invented to extend it.
